item.title: The portfolio case for owning luxury real estate in both Miami and New York
item.author: Bambang Setiawan
item.description:
By Bambang Setiawan

For high-net-worth individuals considering international property investments, the debate between Miami and New York often takes centre stage. However, for some buyers, the question isn’t about choosing one over the other but rather how both cities can complement each other within a diverse property portfolio. Luxury real estate in these iconic locations offers unique benefits, and owning in both could present a strategic opportunity for those looking to balance growth, stability, and lifestyle.

The Appeal of Miami and New York

Miami and New York represent two distinct yet equally compelling markets. Miami is renowned for its year-round sunshine, waterfront properties, and thriving luxury lifestyle scene. It attracts buyers seeking a blend of relaxation and investment potential, particularly in the high-end condo market. Meanwhile, New York remains a global financial hub, offering unparalleled cultural experiences, prestige, and a robust real estate market that has historically shown resilience even during economic downturns.

For investors, Miami’s lower tax environment and growing tech sector make it an attractive option, while New York’s status as a global city ensures long-term demand for prime real estate. Together, these cities provide a balance of stability, growth, and diversification, appealing to those looking to maximise their portfolio’s potential.

Strategic Benefits of Owning in Both Cities

Owning luxury properties in both Miami and New York can offer several strategic advantages. Firstly, diversification reduces risk. Whilst New York’s market is often seen as a safe haven, Miami’s growth potential can provide higher returns. Secondly, the lifestyle benefits are significant. A New York penthouse can serve as a base for business and cultural pursuits, whilst a Miami retreat offers a sunny escape. This dual ownership caters to both professional and personal needs.

Additionally, currency fluctuations and geopolitical factors can impact international investments. Holding assets in two major US cities can help mitigate these risks, providing a hedge against uncertainty. For those with a long-term wealth strategy, this approach ensures flexibility and adaptability in changing market conditions.

Considerations for International Buyers

For UK-based buyers, investing in US luxury real estate requires careful planning. Factors such as exchange rates, tax implications, and financing options should be thoroughly researched. Working with experienced international property specialists and mortgage advisors can help navigate these complexities. It’s also worth considering the legal and regulatory differences between the UK and the US, particularly regarding property ownership and inheritance laws.

Mortgages for international properties may differ from domestic loans, and buyers might explore options such as US dollar-denominated mortgages or leveraging existing assets to fund purchases. Ensuring a clear understanding of all costs, including maintenance, management fees, and local taxes, is essential to make informed decisions.

For those considering luxury real estate investments, Miami and New York offer a compelling combination of opportunities. Diversifying across these two markets could provide both financial and lifestyle benefits, making it a strategy worth exploring for high-net-worth individuals. As with any significant investment, thorough research and professional advice are key to achieving the best outcomes.

item.title: Regulation and redress must work hand in hand if this reform is to deliver for consumers
item.author: Nadya Putri Maharani
item.description:
By Nadya Putri Maharani

Effective regulation in the property sector plays a crucial role in protecting consumers while maintaining professional standards. When implemented correctly, it creates a fair marketplace, builds trust, and ensures accountability. However, regulators often face high expectations from the public while navigating complex relationships with industry professionals. The recent government proposal to introduce independent regulation for property agents marks a significant step forward in raising standards across the sector.

The importance of regulation and consumer expectations

Many homeowners mistakenly believe that redress schemes like The Property Ombudsman (TPO) have regulatory powers to sanction agents or close businesses. In reality, such organisations primarily handle complaints and disputes rather than enforcing industry-wide rules. This gap between consumer expectations and actual functions highlights the need for clearer separation—and collaboration—between regulation and redress mechanisms.

Professional regulation typically focuses on:

  • Setting qualification requirements for practitioners
  • Monitoring compliance with industry standards
  • Taking disciplinary action when necessary

Redress schemes, meanwhile, serve as an accessible route for consumers to resolve specific disputes. The confusion between these functions suggests that future reforms should prioritise simpler pathways for consumers seeking assistance.

Creating a joined-up system for consumer protection

For the proposed regulation of property agents to deliver meaningful benefits, it must work seamlessly with existing complaint handling procedures. Homeowners should not need to navigate complex institutional distinctions when facing issues with property transactions or lettings.

Key considerations for effective reform include:

  • Clear escalation paths between complaint resolution and regulatory oversight
  • Efficient information sharing between different parts of the system
  • Minimising duplication while ensuring no gaps in consumer protection

TPO's experience handling initial enquiries before they become formal complaints provides valuable insight into common consumer concerns. This data could help shape more responsive regulation that addresses real-world problems in the property market.

The property sector's evolution towards better consumer protection represents an opportunity to build a system where regulation and redress complement each other effectively. When implemented thoughtfully, these changes could lead to higher professional standards while giving homeowners greater confidence in property transactions. The success of reforms will depend on how well different components integrate to serve consumer needs simply and efficiently.

item.title: Student lets and Ground 4A: using holding deposits to reserve properties early
item.author: Rizky Aditya Pratama
item.description:
By Rizky Aditya Pratama

The Renters Rights Act 2025 has introduced significant changes for student landlords in England, particularly around tenancy agreements and early termination. With the removal of section 21 'no fault' evictions and new restrictions on rent payments in advance, many landlords are exploring alternative approaches – including the strategic use of holding deposits to secure student properties earlier in the academic cycle.

New challenges for student landlords

The legislation presents two main difficulties for those letting to students. Firstly, landlords can no longer request multiple months' rent upfront as security, potentially increasing financial risk. Secondly, students can now serve just two months' notice to quit, potentially leaving landlords with voids during term time if replacement tenants aren't found.

Whilst Ground 4A was introduced as a specific possession ground for student tenancies, its usefulness is limited. The provision only applies where the tenancy duration is six months or less – conflicting with the traditional academic year lettings that both students and landlords typically prefer.

The holding deposit solution

Some landlords have considered creative workarounds like unsigned tenancy agreements or 'agreement to let' documents, but these approaches may invalidate Ground 4A rights. A more compliant solution lies in properly structured holding deposits.

Current regulations permit holding deposits of up to one week's rent, even for joint student tenancies. Crucially, the standard 15-day holding period can be extended by written agreement. This allows landlords to:

  • Secure properties for students many months in advance
  • Avoid creating a binding tenancy agreement prematurely
  • Maintain eligibility to use Ground 4A if needed

For example, a landlord negotiating with students in October for a July tenancy start could set a holding deposit deadline in January – creating a reservation period without establishing a full tenancy.

Key considerations

When using extended holding deposits, landlords should ensure:

  • The holding deposit agreement clearly states it doesn't create a tenancy
  • Any extended deadline is properly documented
  • The deposit amount never exceeds one week's rent
  • Standard deposit protection rules are followed

With careful planning, holding deposits can help bridge the gap between student renting patterns and the new regulatory framework, whilst protecting landlords' interests within the law.

item.title: Comings & Goings
item.author: Sri Wahyuni Astuti
item.description:
By Sri Wahyuni Astuti

Two prominent UK property firms have announced significant leadership changes this month, with Knight Frank promoting a long-standing partner and Vistry Partnerships preparing for a senior retirement after four decades in the sector.

Knight Frank elevates Islington veteran

Sophie McCarthy has been appointed as head of sales at Knight Frank's Islington office, where she has worked since the branch first opened in 2012. The newly-promoted partner brings 17 years of experience with the agency, having begun her career in the firm's St John's Wood branch before helping establish the Islington operation.

In her elevated role, McCarthy will oversee residential sales across the North London office while collaborating with regional partners and Knight Frank's wider London network. The estate agent highlighted her deep understanding of Islington's property market and proven track record in client relationship building as key factors in the appointment.

The promotion reflects Knight Frank's strategy of developing internal talent, with regional partner Jon Reynolds praising McCarthy's "outstanding results" and market expertise. Industry observers may view this as a stabilising move amid fluctuating London property prices, ensuring continuity of service in a competitive local market.

Vistry prepares for leadership transition

Meanwhile, Vistry Group has announced the planned retirement of partnerships chief Stephen Teagle after 40 years in the housing sector. Catherine Raynsford, currently at Legal & General Affordable Homes, will succeed him as group partnerships director from January 2027.

Teagle will remain during the first quarter of next year to oversee the transition before departing at the end of March. His career has spanned both housing associations and plc housebuilders, including 18 years at Galliford Try before its housing operations merged with Bovis Homes to form Vistry.

This leadership change follows earlier appointments at the £4bn-turnover housebuilder, including a new chair in March and group chief executive in April. The transition comes as Vistry navigates a challenging period, having recently reported substantial losses amid broader sector pressures.

For homeowners and investors tracking the UK property sector, these high-profile moves highlight how established firms are balancing continuity with fresh leadership perspectives during a period of economic uncertainty. Both appointments suggest a focus on maintaining strong client relationships while adapting to evolving market conditions.

item.title: Housing market faces fresh squeeze as mortgage rates hit three-year high
item.author: Bambang Setiawan
item.description:
By Bambang Setiawan

The UK housing market is currently navigating a challenging period, with falling house prices, rising mortgage rates, and political debates over property taxation creating uncertainty for buyers and sellers alike. Recent data highlights a slowdown in activity, with mortgage approvals and transactions below their long-term averages, whilst borrowing costs have reached their highest levels in three years.

Mortgage Rates Hit Three-Year High

Mortgage rates have surged in recent months, with the average five-year fixed rate reaching 6% in October, its highest level since September 2023, according to Moneyfacts. This increase has been driven by rising inflation expectations, partly linked to geopolitical tensions in the Middle East. Mortgage offers typically last for up to six months, meaning the full impact of higher rates is gradually filtering through to the market.

Bank of England figures reveal that mortgage approvals in August were 14% below their five-year average, suggesting a slowdown in buyer activity. Similarly, HMRC data shows property transactions remained broadly flat compared to historical benchmarks. Experts warn that transaction numbers could decline further in the final months of the year as more borrowers face higher borrowing costs.

Political Uncertainty Adds to Market Challenges

Political debates over property taxation are adding another layer of uncertainty to the market. The Conservative Party has pledged to scrap the proposed council tax surcharge on homes valued at £2 million or more, whilst also announcing plans to abolish inheritance tax on primary residences. In contrast, Labour is advocating for higher taxes on expensive properties, whilst Reform UK opposes new taxes without committing to reverse the surcharge.

These competing policies are particularly affecting the upper end of the market, where buyers and sellers are facing increased uncertainty. With the Budget approaching, the future of property taxation remains unclear, potentially impacting market confidence further.

What Does This Mean for Homebuyers?

For those considering entering the housing market or remortgaging, the current environment presents both challenges and opportunities. Whilst higher mortgage rates may increase borrowing costs, falling house prices could provide some relief for buyers. Homeowners may wish to explore their options carefully, seeking advice to understand how rising rates and political changes could affect their financial plans.

As inflation concerns persist, borrowing costs are likely to remain elevated in the near term. Market analysts have noted that attention has shifted from crude oil supplies to shortages of refined products, particularly diesel, which could further impact inflation and, in turn, mortgage rates.

In summary, the UK housing market is facing a complex mix of economic and political factors, creating a cautious outlook for the remainder of the year. Borrowers and homeowners may need to stay informed and consider their options carefully in this evolving landscape.

item.title: Property consultancy moves office as it plans further hires
item.author: Bambang Setiawan
item.description:
By Bambang Setiawan

Bradley Hall has recently relocated its Manchester operations to new, larger premises on King Street as part of plans to expand its property consultancy team. The move follows significant growth in the firm's valuation services and will provide capacity for further recruitment across both residential and commercial property sectors.

Expanding team and services

The Manchester office, serving Greater Manchester and surrounding counties including Cheshire and Lancashire, has already welcomed three new surveyors to its ranks. Recent appointments include graduate surveyor Sienna Baker, associate director Benjamin Riddle and chartered surveyor Matthew Beswick. Further recruitment is expected in the coming months as the firm capitalises on growing demand for valuation services.

The consultancy provides a comprehensive range of property services including residential and commercial valuations, working with lenders, developers and private clients. Its broader operations span estate agency, lettings, auctions and property management across 13 UK offices.

Strategic growth in the North West

Charlotte Williams, associate director leading the Manchester team, noted the relocation marks an important milestone in the office's development. The new premises offer improved collaborative spaces and room for expansion while serving an increasing client base across the region.

Neil Hart, Bradley Hall's chief executive, emphasised the firm's people-focused growth strategy. The enhanced facilities are designed to support recruitment of skilled surveyors while meeting rising demand for valuation services in both residential and commercial markets.

Founded in 1988, Bradley Hall has evolved from its North East origins to become a national property consultancy. Its Manchester expansion reflects the firm's commitment to strengthening its presence in key regional markets, with particular focus on valuation services that support lending decisions and property transactions.

For homeowners and property professionals in the North West, the firm's growth may signal increased local capacity for valuation and surveying services. Those requiring property valuations might find it worthwhile researching local providers with expanding teams and specialist expertise in their area.

item.title: Landlord Law Newsround #457
item.author: Bambang Setiawan
item.description:
By Bambang Setiawan

The UK’s private rented sector is undergoing significant changes, with new developments and challenges emerging for landlords and tenants alike. From regulatory updates to shifting tenant demographics, here’s a closer look at the latest trends shaping the property market.

New PRS Ombudsman Scheme Expected by 2028

The introduction of a compulsory Private Rented Sector (PRS) Landlord Ombudsman has been confirmed, with the scheme anticipated to launch in 2028. While the Government has yet to select an operator for the service, it is expected that nearly all private landlords will be required to join. This new initiative is separate from the existing voluntary membership offered by the Housing Ombudsman. The move aims to improve accountability and dispute resolution within the rental market, offering tenants greater protection and landlords clearer guidelines.

Rising Demand for Out-of-Hours Tenant Support

Recent research highlights a growing trend of tenants reaching out to landlords and letting agents outside standard working hours. According to LightWork AI, 43% of tenant communications now occur outside the traditional 9am to 5pm window, with 49% being emails or portal enquiries and 28% phone calls. This shift places additional pressure on agents and landlords, who are increasingly expected to be available around the clock. Leonard Charlton, co-founder of LightWork AI, noted that this constant demand is contributing to burnout within the industry, making it harder to retain skilled professionals.

Changing Tenant Demographics and Aspirations

The profile of the average tenant is evolving, with many renters facing barriers to homeownership. A survey by the TDS Charitable Foundation reveals that 76% of renters aspire to buy their own home, yet 44% now expect to rent for the rest of their lives. This has led to longer tenancies, with the average duration now standing at 4.7 years, up from 3.7 years a decade ago. Additionally, there is growing interest in social housing, particularly among older tenants, families, and those with health conditions. The findings underscore the need for housing policies to adapt to these shifts, ensuring renters have access to a wider range of options beyond private renting.

Energy Efficiency Concerns in the Rental Market

Energy efficiency is becoming a key consideration for tenants, with 42% factoring it into their rental decisions. However, many landlords are struggling to meet EPC (Energy Performance Certificate) targets, particularly as the Government pushes for greener housing standards. This gap highlights the challenges faced by landlords in upgrading properties to meet evolving expectations, while tenants increasingly prioritise sustainability and cost-saving measures.

As the rental market continues to evolve, landlords, tenants, and policymakers alike will need to navigate these changes to ensure a fair and sustainable future for the sector.

item.title: Is the UK property market really dead?
item.author: Nadya Putri Maharani
item.description:
By Nadya Putri Maharani

Amidst headlines declaring the UK property market as stagnant or even "dead," a closer look at the latest data reveals a more nuanced picture. Whilst the market may not be booming, there are still significant opportunities for both buyers and sellers. Understanding the current trends, from new listings to sales agreed, can help homeowners and estate agents navigate this evolving landscape.

Current Market Trends

Recent statistics show that the UK property market remains active, albeit at a slower pace compared to previous years. In week 39, there were 34,800 new listings, slightly down from 35,300 the previous week. Year-to-date figures indicate 1.406 million new listings, which is marginally below 2025’s figures but 2% higher than 2024 and nearly 10% above 2023. This suggests a steady flow of properties entering the market, offering buyers a range of options.

item.title: Property firms expelled from The Property Ombudsman
item.author: Rizky Aditya Pratama
item.description:
By Rizky Aditya Pratama

Three property firms have been removed from The Property Ombudsman (TPO) scheme following their failure to pay compensation awards issued in response to consumer complaints. The businesses, which include two letting agents and a surveying company, were expelled after refusing to settle payments ranging from £100 to £800. TPO’s independent Finance, Performance and Compliance Committee reviewed the cases before enforcing the expulsions, emphasising that its rulings are binding for all registered firms.

Details of the Cases

Musgrove & Co, based in North Walsham and registered as Musco Property Limited, faced a complaint from a landlord regarding its handling of a tenancy. The landlord alleged that the agency refused to transfer a holding deposit, made errors in the tenancy agreement, and failed to provide a suitable replacement tenant. Additionally, the firm did not respond to a formal complaint, prompting the landlord to arrange the tenancy directly with the tenants. TPO upheld the complaint and ordered Musgrove & Co to pay £300, but the firm failed to provide evidence during the investigation and did not settle the award.

Tothill Residential Surveying Ltd, located in Mundon, was involved in a dispute with a buyer who paid £500 for a survey. The buyer claimed the firm failed to deliver the survey report and mishandled their subsequent complaint. TPO reviewed the case and directed the company to pay £800 in compensation, which remained unpaid, leading to its expulsion from the scheme.

Coles Property Management, registered as C.P.M (NW) Limited in Blackpool, faced a complaint from a landlord who had terminated its management agreement for two rental properties. The landlord reported delays in transferring tenants’ deposits to a new agent and a failure to forward rent payments mistakenly sent to Coles. TPO identified additional communication failings and ordered the firm to pay £100, which was not settled.

TPO’s Stance on Compliance

Chief Ombudsman Lesley Horton stressed that Ombudsman awards are not optional and that registered businesses are expected to comply with decisions. She explained that expulsion is always a last resort, with TPO working closely with firms throughout the compliance process to encourage resolution. However, failure to adhere to rulings leaves TPO with no choice but to remove businesses from the scheme.

This action serves as a reminder to property firms of the importance of adhering to consumer protection standards and fulfilling their obligations under the TPO scheme. For consumers, it highlights the value of using TPO-registered businesses, which are held accountable for their actions.

item.title: Awaab’s Law moves closer for agents as repair deadline shake-up begins
item.author: Sri Wahyuni Astuti
item.description:
By Sri Wahyuni Astuti

The government has launched a consultation on extending Awaab’s Law to the private rented sector, which could introduce legally binding repair deadlines for letting agents and landlords in England. This follows the legislation’s introduction in social housing after the tragic death of two-year-old Awaab Ishak from prolonged exposure to damp and mould in 2020.

What Awaab’s Law means for private rentals

Currently, private landlords must address hazards like damp, mould and structural risks under the Housing Health and Safety Rating System (HHSRS). However, Awaab’s Law would introduce fixed timescales for investigating and repairing serious issues in private tenancies. The consultation will determine how these rules apply to the private rented sector, with potential implications for:

  • Response times for urgent hazards
  • Deadlines for written repair plans
  • Timescales for completing necessary works

In social housing, the law requires landlords to make dangerous properties safe within 24 hours, investigate other hazards within 10 working days, and complete urgent repairs within five days. Similar requirements could soon apply to private rentals, though the government acknowledges the sector’s different challenges.

Industry concerns about implementation

The National Residential Landlords Association (NRLA) supports the principle of Awaab’s Law but highlights practical differences between social and private renting. Unlike large housing associations, most private landlords lack in-house maintenance teams and may struggle to secure tradespeople at short notice.

Key considerations in the consultation include:

  • Whether private landlords should have slightly longer response times
  • How to handle situations where tenants deny access
  • Potential exemptions for smaller landlords

Housing campaigners argue that consistent standards should apply across all tenures, while landlord groups emphasise the need for workable requirements. The government will weigh these perspectives before finalising the rules.

This reform forms part of the broader Renters’ Rights Act, which aims to improve standards in England’s private rented sector. With damp and mould affecting many rental properties, the changes could significantly impact how landlords and agents handle repair requests. The consultation runs until [date], with new regulations expected to follow in 2024.

item.title: Major property firm withdraws from London’s ‘broken’ housing market
item.author: Bambang Setiawan
item.description:
By Bambang Setiawan

Taylor Wimpey, one of the UK’s leading housebuilders, has announced it will cease new developments in London once its current projects are complete. The decision highlights growing concerns over the viability of housebuilding in the capital, with the firm’s chief executive, Jennie Daly, describing London’s housing market as “fundamentally broken”. This move adds to the mounting pressure on the city’s ability to meet its housing targets, amid rising costs and regulatory challenges.

The Challenges Facing London’s Housing Market

Taylor Wimpey’s decision reflects broader issues impacting developers in London and the South East. The firm cited weaker buyer demand, higher construction costs, and stringent planning requirements as key factors making new schemes economically unviable. Mortgage rate increases have further exacerbated affordability challenges, particularly in a city where property prices are already significantly higher than the national average.

Other developers have also scaled back their presence in the region. Vistry, for example, recently announced it would exit open-market housebuilding in the South East as part of a wider restructuring. The Home Builders Federation has echoed these concerns, describing London as a “no-go zone for housing investment”. These developments raise questions about the capital’s ability to deliver the 88,000 new homes required annually to meet government targets.

Regulatory Pressures and Affordable Housing

London’s affordable housing rules have become a particular point of contention for developers. The mayor’s planning framework mandates that developments using the fast-track route must provide at least 35% affordable housing, subject to policy requirements. However, this has been criticised for adding to the financial burden on developers, particularly when combined with other regulatory costs.

Jennie Daly also highlighted the impact of late-stage viability reviews, which can require developers to increase their affordable housing contributions if a scheme proves more profitable than initially forecast. This, she argued, creates uncertainty and discourages investment. “If it proves that I have made a good bet and my scheme is profitable, I’d have to increase the level of [affordable housing] contribution. For many, that has just proven too ambitious,” Daly explained.

The rejection of Berkeley Group’s plans for hundreds of homes in Peckham further underscores the challenges developers face in navigating London’s planning system. Such setbacks have led to calls for a review of the regulatory framework to ensure it supports, rather than hinders, housing delivery.

As developers continue to reassess their involvement in London, the capital’s housing crisis shows no signs of easing. Policymakers and industry leaders may need to work together to address the underlying issues and restore confidence in the market.

item.title: Can You Complete on a House Before Christmas
item.author: Bambang Setiawan
item.description:
By Bambang Setiawan

For many homebuyers, completing a property purchase before Christmas holds particular appeal. Moving into a new home before the festive season can bring both practical advantages and emotional rewards. However, whilst it's certainly possible to complete in time for Christmas, several factors influence whether this becomes achievable in individual cases.

The Challenges of Christmas Completion

The December property market often sees heightened activity as buyers aim to settle before the holidays. This seasonal surge can create bottlenecks in the conveyancing process. Homebuyers might face delays with:

  • Surveyor availability during the busy period
  • Local authority searches taking longer than usual
  • Solicitors handling increased workloads
  • Mortgage lenders processing higher volumes of applications
  • Chain complications if other parties have inflexible deadlines

Whilst estate agents and conveyancers typically work right up to Christmas Eve, unexpected delays can push completion dates into the new year. Borrowers might consider starting the process as early as possible in autumn to improve their chances of meeting a pre-Christmas deadline.

Speeding Up The Process

Homeowners hoping for a festive move may wish to explore ways to potentially accelerate their purchase:

  • Opting for a mortgage broker who can help identify lenders with faster processing times
  • Considering digital conveyancing services which may offer quicker turnaround
  • Requesting priority searches from the local authority (where available)
  • Being immediately responsive to all requests from solicitors and lenders
  • Choosing a property with no upward chain where possible

It's worth noting that cash buyers or those purchasing through auction typically have more control over completion dates. However, even in these cases, legal processes still require sufficient time.

Managing Expectations

Whilst a pre-Christmas completion remains possible, setting realistic expectations proves crucial. The average conveyancing process takes between 8-12 weeks, meaning purchases started in October have the best chance of completing before the holidays. However, each transaction remains unique, with some completing faster and others taking longer.

Borrowers might find it helpful to discuss timeline expectations with their solicitor early in the process. Some firms offer Christmas completion guarantees, though these usually come with specific conditions about when instructions are received and how promptly clients respond to queries.

For those who don't complete in time, there may be advantages to waiting until January when the market typically quietens down. Whatever the outcome, keeping communication open with all parties involved remains key to navigating the seasonal property market successfully.

item.title: How An Investment Platform Can Make Managed Investing More Accessible
item.author: Bambang Setiawan
item.description:
By Bambang Setiawan

For many savers, traditional savings accounts have long been a go-to option for stashing away money. However, with inflation often outpacing the interest rates offered by these accounts, they may not be the most effective way to grow wealth over time. Meanwhile, venturing into the stock market can feel intimidating, especially for those without prior investment experience. Historically, professional wealth management was reserved for individuals with significant capital, but thanks to digital advancements, managed investing has become more accessible than ever.

The Shift Towards Digital Investment Platforms

In recent years, digital investment platforms have emerged as a game-changer for everyday savers. These platforms leverage technology to provide access to institutional-grade investment strategies, previously only available to high-net-worth individuals. By automating processes and reducing overhead costs, they offer a more affordable and user-friendly alternative to traditional wealth management services. This shift has opened the door for a broader audience to explore managed investing, even with modest sums of money.

Benefits of Managed Investing Through Digital Platforms

Managed investment platforms come with several advantages that appeal to both novice and experienced investors. Here are some key benefits:

  • Accessibility: Many platforms have low minimum investment requirements, making it possible for individuals to start investing with smaller amounts of capital.
  • Expertise: Investors gain access to professional portfolio management, often tailored to their risk tolerance and financial goals.
  • Convenience: These platforms typically offer user-friendly interfaces and automated features, simplifying the investment process.
  • Cost Efficiency: By eliminating the need for in-person advisors, digital platforms often charge lower fees compared to traditional wealth management services.

For those looking to diversify their financial portfolio beyond standard savings accounts, managed investment platforms could be a worthwhile option to explore. They provide an opportunity to potentially achieve higher returns whilst mitigating some of the risks associated with direct stock market investments.

As with any financial decision, it is important to conduct thorough research and consider seeking independent advice to ensure the chosen platform aligns with individual financial goals and circumstances. Managed investing through digital platforms offers a modern solution for those seeking to grow their wealth in a structured and accessible way.

item.title: ‘Pain in the post’ for housing market as buyer demand weakens and mortgage costs jump
item.author: Nadya Putri Maharani
item.description:
By Nadya Putri Maharani

The UK housing market showed signs of slowing momentum in September, as rising mortgage costs and economic pressures weighed on buyer confidence. According to the Royal Institution of Chartered Surveyors (RICS), buyer enquiries declined for the first time since March, whilst agreed sales also softened. These findings highlight the challenges facing homeowners and prospective buyers amidst higher borrowing costs and uncertain market conditions.

Buyer demand weakens as affordability concerns grow

RICS reported a net balance of -22% for new buyer enquiries in September, down from -18% in August. This marks the first decline in six months, although it remains an improvement compared to the -41% recorded earlier in the year. Agreed sales also saw a slight dip, with the balance falling to -18% from -16% in August. Expectations for sales over the next three months also deteriorated, reflecting growing caution among buyers.

However, the latest Lloyds House Price Index paints a slightly different picture, with new buyer enquiries reportedly reaching their highest level since February. Whilst house prices remained flat in September, both monthly and annually, the average property price stood at £298,441. Prices also slipped by 0.2% on a quarterly basis, suggesting a cooling market.

Mortgage costs rise sharply, squeezing affordability

Higher mortgage rates have significantly increased the financial burden for borrowers. According to Moneyfacts, the average five-year fixed mortgage rate has climbed to 6.00%, compared to 4.91% at the start of 2026. For a typical £250,000 mortgage over 25 years, this translates to monthly repayments of around £1,611—an increase of £163 per month or £1,956 annually.

Rachel Springall, a finance expert at Moneyfactscompare.co.uk, noted that affordability remains a key challenge for buyers. “Higher mortgage rates and the rising cost of living are creating a painful affordability squeeze for new buyers,” she said. Whilst softer house prices might offer some relief, higher borrowing costs could offset any potential savings.

First-time buyers with larger deposits may find opportunities in a cooling market, but the overall affordability boost could be undermined by rising mortgage rates. Springall added that weaker demand might improve bargaining power for buyers, though this advantage could be limited by the broader financial pressures.

Despite these challenges, there are signs of more homes coming to the market, which could provide greater choice for buyers. However, the combination of higher mortgage costs and subdued demand suggests the housing market may face continued headwinds in the months ahead.

For those navigating the current landscape, staying informed about mortgage options and market trends could help in making well-considered decisions. Borrowers might also explore seeking independent financial advice to better understand their options in this evolving environment.

By Rizky Aditya Pratama

Proposed changes to inheritance tax (IHT) and stamp duty by the Conservative Party have sparked mixed reactions from property professionals. Whilst many have welcomed the potential reforms, concerns have been raised about the finer details and how such measures might be funded.

Inheritance Tax Overhaul

The Conservatives have pledged to exempt family homes from inheritance tax, allowing couples to leave an additional £1m tax-free. Kemi Badenoch, during her keynote conference speech, even expressed an ambition to abolish IHT altogether, stating it would happen “as soon as we can afford it.” Estimates suggest these reforms could cost the Treasury approximately £6bn annually.

Timothy Douglas, head of policy and campaigns at Propertymark, described the commitment to remove IHT on family homes as a positive step for homeowners and families planning for the future. However, he emphasised that “the detail will matter,” warning against shifting the tax burden elsewhere. Douglas highlighted the importance of maintaining a stable and accessible housing market, particularly as households continue to face affordability and supply challenges.

Stamp Duty Reforms

Another key proposal is the abolition of stamp duty on primary homes, a move Douglas labelled as “significant.” Stamp duty has long been a major cost for those looking to move, and its removal could potentially stimulate the housing market. However, Douglas cautioned that any replacement tax would need to be carefully considered to avoid unintended consequences.

Trevor Abrahmsohn, managing director of Glentree International, was more enthusiastic about the proposals, describing the potential scrapping of stamp duty as “very welcome.” He argued that high stamp duty rates have historically held back the housing market, trapping capital in property that could otherwise circulate in the economy through retail spending and other activities.

Funding Concerns

Despite the positive reception, questions remain about how these tax cuts would be funded. Abrahmsohn voiced support for the measures but stressed the importance of ensuring they are “properly costed” to avoid unsettling bond markets. Similarly, Douglas urged ministers to collaborate with the property industry to ensure reforms support transactions rather than shifting the tax burden elsewhere.

Whilst the proposed reforms aim to alleviate financial pressures on homeowners and stimulate the housing market, their success will likely depend on careful planning and execution. As property professionals have highlighted, the devil is in the detail.

item.title: Comings & Goings
item.author: Sri Wahyuni Astuti
item.description:
By Sri Wahyuni Astuti

The property market is seeing notable shifts in leadership roles, with Chestertons and Savills both announcing key promotions and appointments. These changes reflect the evolving demands of the property sector and the growing importance of specialised expertise in areas such as short lets and private client property management.

Chestertons Promotes Jordana Miles to Head of Short Lets

Chestertons has appointed Jordana Miles as its new head of short lets, a promotion that comes just under a year after she joined the agency as business development manager within the division. In her new role, Miles will oversee short-term lettings, which typically last between two-and-a-half to three months. She will work across Chestertons’ 35 London branches, collaborating with local sales and lettings teams to identify properties suitable for short-term tenancies.

Miles brings a wealth of experience to the role, having spent over five years at Draker Lettings prior to joining Chestertons in October 2025. Her background includes expertise in the short-let markets of Sloane Square, Notting Hill, and Fulham, as well as managing a team of eight negotiators at Draker’s Chelsea and Kensington branch.

Commenting on her appointment, Miles highlighted the benefits of short lets for property owners. “A property can still be well suited to the sales market even if it hasn’t found the right buyer yet,” she said. “Owners don’t necessarily have to leave it empty and absorb the costs while they wait. We can assess the demand for a short let, prepare the property, and generate income whilst keeping the sales strategy in view.”

Katinka Hill, head of lettings at Chestertons, praised Miles for her contributions to the team. “Jordana has been a driving force in our Short Lets team, combining real passion and focus with considerable expertise,” Hill said. “She has a clear grasp of what the service offers owners and occupants alike, and through close collaboration with colleagues across the business, she has made it easier than ever for clients to use this flexible option.”

Savills Appoints Adam De Acetis as Director in Property Management Division

Meanwhile, Savills has strengthened its Property Management division with the appointment of Adam De Acetis as a director. De Acetis will focus on expanding the division’s offerings for private clients, including property companies, private investors, family offices, and high-net-worth individuals.

With a background in property management, strategic asset management, lease advisory, and real estate development, De Acetis brings a wealth of experience to his new role. His previous work has included developing asset business plans, overseeing value-add initiatives, and collaborating with landlords and occupiers on portfolio strategies.

At Savills, De Acetis will work alongside the existing team to develop property and portfolio-level strategies for private clients. His appointment underscores Savills’ commitment to enhancing its services for high-net-worth individuals and private investors.

These appointments reflect the growing complexity of the property market, with both Chestertons and Savills investing in specialised talent to meet the needs of their clients. As the sector continues to evolve, such strategic hires could prove instrumental in navigating changes and capitalising on emerging opportunities.

item.title: Property professionals back homebuying reforms as industry calls for action
item.author: Bambang Setiawan
item.description:
By Bambang Setiawan

A recent industry poll has revealed strong support for proposed reforms to the UK homebuying process, with nearly eight in 10 property professionals expressing confidence in their potential to bring positive change. Conducted by Countrywide Surveying Services (CSS), the survey found that 77% of respondents were optimistic about the impact of these reforms, with 18% describing themselves as “very confident” and 59% as “somewhat confident”. Only 2% believed the changes would never materialise.

The Case for Upfront Information

The poll was conducted during a webinar exploring whether providing upfront property information could streamline the buying and selling process. Discussions centred on the benefits of making essential details available earlier in transactions, which could help reduce delays and improve certainty for all parties involved. Matthew Cumber, Managing Director at CSS, highlighted the importance of accessible, shareable information in driving meaningful reform. He emphasised that simply bringing existing checks and documents forward would not be enough; instead, ensuring useful information is available early in a standardised format could transform the process.

Collaboration Across the Industry

Cumber also stressed that successful reform would require collaboration across different sectors of the property industry. He noted that lenders, surveyors, conveyancers, estate agents, brokers, and technology providers must work together to improve the process as a whole, rather than focusing on individual components in isolation. By doing so, he believes the industry could reduce avoidable delays and provide buyers with greater clarity about the properties they are purchasing.

The webinar also touched on the recent appointment of Andy Burnham and its potential impact on the housing market. Opinions were divided, with 36% of attendees believing his appointment would make positive change more likely, while 16% thought it would hinder progress. Nearly half (48%) felt it would make no difference.

Looking Ahead

The discussion underscored a growing consensus that the homebuying process needs improvement, with attention now shifting towards implementation. As the industry seeks to turn ambition into action, homeowners, buyers, and sellers may wish to stay informed about potential changes that could affect their property transactions. With over 300 property professionals, including surveyors, mortgage brokers, and lenders, participating in the webinar, the momentum for reform appears to be building.

For those navigating the property market, keeping an eye on developments in this area could prove valuable, particularly as reforms aim to create a more efficient and transparent homebuying experience.

item.title: BTR investment so far in 2026 hits £4.2bn
item.author: Bambang Setiawan
item.description:
By Bambang Setiawan

The Build-to-Rent (BTR) sector in the UK has seen significant growth in 2026, with a reported £4.2 billion invested so far this year. This surge highlights the increasing demand for rental properties, particularly in the single-family housing market, as investors continue to recognise the long-term potential of the BTR model.

The Rise of Build-to-Rent

The BTR sector has become a cornerstone of the UK property market, offering purpose-built rental homes designed to meet the needs of modern tenants. The £4.2 billion investment milestone underscores the sector’s resilience and attractiveness to both institutional and private investors. Single-family housing, in particular, has emerged as a key focus, catering to families and long-term renters seeking stability and quality accommodation.

This trend reflects broader shifts in housing preferences, with more individuals opting for rental solutions over homeownership due to affordability challenges and lifestyle flexibility. The BTR model provides tenants with professionally managed properties, often including amenities such as communal spaces, gyms, and concierge services, enhancing the overall rental experience.

What This Means for the Property Market

The influx of investment into the BTR sector is reshaping the UK property landscape. For landlords and investors, the growing demand for rental properties presents opportunities to diversify portfolios and achieve stable returns. Meanwhile, tenants benefit from increased choice and higher standards of living, as BTR developments often prioritise quality and tenant satisfaction.

For those considering property investment, the BTR sector’s strong performance in 2026 may serve as a compelling indicator of its potential. However, it’s essential to conduct thorough research and seek professional advice to ensure any investment aligns with individual financial goals and market conditions.

As the BTR sector continues to flourish, it could play a pivotal role in addressing the UK’s housing needs, offering a viable alternative to traditional homeownership and contributing to a more dynamic rental market.

item.title: Nearly a third of rental listings secured tenant in Q3
item.author: Nadya Putri Maharani
item.description:
By Nadya Putri Maharani

The UK rental market has shown signs of resilience in the third quarter of 2023, with nearly a third of rental listings successfully securing tenants. According to data from LegalforLandlords, demand for rental properties experienced modest growth during this period, though regional variations highlight significant differences across local markets.

Rental Market Shows Steady Demand

Despite economic uncertainties, the rental market has remained relatively stable, with approximately 30% of listed properties finding tenants in Q3. This figure suggests a continued appetite for rental accommodation, driven by factors such as rising mortgage costs and shifting housing preferences. Whilst the overall demand has seen a slight uptick, the pace of growth varies depending on location and property type.

Regional Variations in the Rental Market

The data also underscores notable disparities between local markets. In some areas, demand has surged, leading to quicker lettings and competitive rental prices. Conversely, other regions have experienced slower activity, with properties taking longer to secure tenants. These variations may be influenced by factors such as local employment opportunities, affordability, and the availability of rental stock. Landlords and property investors might consider these regional trends when making decisions about their portfolios.

What Does This Mean for Landlords and Tenants?

For landlords, the findings highlight the importance of understanding local market dynamics. Properties in high-demand areas could see quicker lettings and potentially higher rental yields, whilst those in slower markets may require more competitive pricing or enhanced marketing strategies. Tenants, on the other hand, may find opportunities in regions with less competition, potentially securing more favourable rental terms.

As the UK rental market continues to evolve, staying informed about regional trends and market conditions could prove valuable for both landlords and tenants alike. With demand holding steady, albeit with localised differences, the coming months may offer further insights into the direction of the rental sector.

item.title: More buildings need cladding remediation
item.author: Rizky Aditya Pratama
item.description:
By Rizky Aditya Pratama

The issue of unsafe cladding on residential buildings continues to be a pressing concern across the UK, with thousands of properties still requiring remediation work. Despite some progress in addressing the problem, many homeowners and landlords face ongoing uncertainty regarding the safety and valuation of their properties.

Cladding Remediation Progress

Since the Grenfell Tower tragedy in 2017, significant efforts have been made to identify and remediate buildings with unsafe cladding. The government has introduced various funding schemes to support the removal of hazardous materials, particularly in high-rise buildings. However, the scale of the problem remains substantial, with thousands of residential properties still under scrutiny. Whilst some buildings have undergone remediation, the process is often lengthy and complex, leaving many homeowners in limbo.

Impact on Homeowners and Buyers

The presence of unsafe cladding can have far-reaching consequences for homeowners and prospective buyers. Properties with unresolved cladding issues may face difficulties in securing mortgages, as lenders often require evidence of remediation before approving loans. Additionally, homeowners might find their properties devalued or unsellable until the necessary work is completed. For those living in affected buildings, the uncertainty can lead to stress and financial strain.

Homeowners may wish to stay informed about their building’s cladding status and explore available support options. It could be worth contacting the building’s management company or local authority for updates on remediation plans. Borrowers considering purchasing a property in a high-rise building might also consider requesting detailed information about the cladding materials and any remediation work carried out.

Government Initiatives and Support

The government has introduced several initiatives to assist with cladding remediation, including the Building Safety Fund and the Cladding Safety Scheme. These programmes aim to provide financial support for the removal of unsafe cladding, particularly in buildings over 18 metres tall. However, concerns have been raised about the speed and efficiency of these schemes, with some homeowners reporting delays in accessing funding.

For those affected, it might be helpful to seek professional advice to navigate the complexities of cladding remediation. Mortgage brokers and financial advisers could provide guidance on how to manage the financial implications and explore potential solutions.

Whilst progress has been made, the cladding crisis remains a significant challenge for the UK property market. Continued efforts from the government, industry stakeholders, and homeowners will be crucial in resolving this issue and restoring confidence in the safety of residential buildings.
